passages.quote:
Before you dismiss an employee

Dismissal is when an employer ends an employee’s contract. If you are considering dismissal, you must have a valid reason and act reasonably.

Read about Dismissing an employee.

When dismissal may be unfair

A dismissal may be unfair if:

you did not have a fair reason for dismissing the employee

the reason did not justify dismissal

you did not follow a fair procedure

the reason was automatically unfair; for example, dismissing someone because of pregnancy or family leave, trade union activity, whistleblowing or raising a health and safety concern

Qualifying period and changes from 1 January 2027

For dismissals with an effective date of termination before 1 January 2027, an employee will normally need at least 2 years’ continuous employment to claim ‘ordinary’ unfair dismissal.

From 1 January 2027, this will reduce to 6 months. The change applies in England, Scotland and Wales, but not Northern Ireland where legislation relating to unfair dismissal is devolved.

Some protections, including protection against discrimination and automatically unfair dismissal for certain reasons, do not require this qualifying period.

Read about the changes to unfair dismissal rights.

Constructive dismissal and wrongful dismissal

Constructive dismissal is when an employee resigns because they believe the employer seriously breached their employment contract.

Wrongful dismissal is different from unfair dismissal. It is a breach of the employee’s employment contract, for example if you do not give them the notice or notice pay they are entitled to.

If the employee appeals

The employee may appeal against their dismissal if they believe:

the decision was wrong or too severe

the procedure was unfair

there is new evidence that should be considered

Where possible, someone not involved in the original decision should hear the appeal.

You should:

review the original decision and the procedure followed

consider any new evidence

investigate further if necessary

tell the employee the outcome in writing

If the employee makes an employment tribunal claim

An employee may make an employment tribunal claim if they believe they were unfairly, constructively or wrongfully dismissed.

Different eligibility rules and time limits apply depending on the type of claim.

If a tribunal finds that an employee was unfairly dismissed, it may order the employer to:

give the employee their previous job back, known as reinstatement

employ them in another suitable job, known as re-engagement

pay compensation

Read more about Being taken to an employment tribunal.
